## Learning objectives

Students should leave able to:

- Apply the *grammar of graphics* framework to construct statistical plots
- Build the **5 named graphs** (scatterplots, linegraphs, histograms, boxplots, barplots) using `ggplot2`
- Modify aesthetic properties of a plot (color, size, transparency, position)
- Use *facets* to split a plot into panels by a categorical variable

## Common stuck points

_Drawn from the chapter's own Quick check distractors. Each Q lists the misconception each WRONG option encodes &mdash; if a student picks (a) when the answer is (c), here's what they're probably thinking._

### Q1. Which component of the grammar of graphics is responsible for telling `ggplot2` *what kind* of mark to draw (points, bars, lines)?

**Correct: (c)** &mdash; `geom_*()` functions specify the visual mark; `aes()` is the mapping between data and visual properties; `data` is the data frame.

**Likely traps:**

- **(a) data** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(b) aesthetic mapping (`aes`)** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(d) facet** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_

### Q2. Why does `ggplot(data = flights, mapping = aes(x = dep_delay, y = arr_delay))` produce a blank plot?

**Correct: (b)** &mdash; Without a `geom_*()` layer, `ggplot2` has no instructions for *what* to draw. Add `+ geom_point()` (or another geom) to see the result.

**Likely traps:**

- **(a) The data frame is missing** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(c) `dep_delay` and `arr_delay` aren't variables in `flights`** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(d) The `+` operator is missing** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_

### Q3. Which named graph is most appropriate for visualizing the *distribution* of a single numerical variable?

**Correct: (c)** &mdash; Histograms show the distribution of one numerical variable. Barplots are for categorical variables; scatterplots show two numerical variables; linegraphs are for sequential x-axis data.

**Likely traps:**

- **(a) Scatterplot** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(b) Linegraph** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(d) Barplot** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_

### Q4. A student writes `geom_point(aes(alpha = 0.2))` expecting all points to be 20% opaque. Instead, they get an unexpected legend showing alpha values. Why?

**Correct: (b)** &mdash; **Constants belong OUTSIDE `aes()`.** `aes(alpha = 0.2)` says "map the (nonexistent) variable `0.2` to alpha". The fix: `geom_point(alpha = 0.2)` *sets* alpha as a constant. Same logic for `color`, `size`, `shape`, etc.

**Likely traps:**

- **(a) `aes()` always creates a legend** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(c) Alpha must be between 0 and 1** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(d) `geom_point()` doesn't support alpha** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_

### Q5. What is the difference between `geom_bar()` and `geom_col()`?

**Correct: (b)** &mdash; Use `geom_bar()` when each row in your data is one observation to be tallied (e.g., one row per flight). Use `geom_col()` when the data is already summarized (you have explicit `y` values).

**Likely traps:**

- **(a) They're identical** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(c) `geom_col()` makes a column chart only; `geom_bar()` makes a row chart** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(d) `geom_col()` is deprecated** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_

### Q6. A pie chart shows market share for 5 companies. The slices look similar in size. The chapter argues this is a poor choice because:

**Correct: (b)** &mdash; Naomi Robbins (and many others) point out: angles are hard to judge accurately. Bar lengths are easy. A bar chart of the same data lets the reader compare values at a glance.

**Likely traps:**

- **(a) Pie charts are always wrong** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(c) R doesn't render pie charts well** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(d) Pie charts use too much ink** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_

### Q7. In `ggplot()`, why must the `+` come at the **end** of a line, not the beginning of the next?

**Correct: (b)** &mdash; R reads code line by line. Ending a line with `+` tells the parser the statement isn't complete. Starting a line with `+` would make R think the previous line was complete and now you're starting a fresh expression that begins with `+` (an error).

**Likely traps:**

- **(a) Convention only** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(c) RStudio adds it automatically** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(d) Both placements are valid** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_

### Q8. A scatterplot of `dep_delay` vs `arr_delay` shows a dense black blob near (0, 0). Which technique does **NOT** address overplotting?

**Correct: (d)** &mdash; Bins are a histogram concept; scatterplots don't have bins. The other three are real overplotting remedies — alpha makes density visible, jitter spreads coincident points, subsetting reduces overlap.

**Likely traps:**

- **(a) Setting `alpha = 0.1` for transparency** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(b) Using `geom_jitter()` to perturb each point slightly** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(c) Subsetting the data to fewer observations** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_

### Q9. What does `+ facet_wrap(~ origin)` do?

**Correct: (b)** &mdash; Faceting splits one plot into a grid of panels by a categorical variable. Distinct from coloring (which overlays groups on one set of axes) and from filtering (which drops data).

**Likely traps:**

- **(a) Plots all data colored by `origin`** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(c) Filters the data to one origin** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(d) Sorts the data by `origin` level** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_

### Q10. In a side-by-side boxplot of wind speed by month, you see many small dots above the upper whiskers. What do they represent?

**Correct: (b)** &mdash; Boxplot dots beyond whiskers are statistical outliers under the IQR rule. They're not necessarily errors — just values unusually far from the bulk of the data.

**Likely traps:**

- **(a) Errors in the data** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(c) Mean values** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
- **(d) Confidence intervals** &mdash; _(why this is tempting: ________________)_
